notes: Wednesday 4 Nov 2026 world issue (Taipei ~08:00). Window: Tue 3 Nov (US Election Day; results not yet known at press time). Economy: US tech stocks bounce after AI-spending scare; Disney plans thousands of layoffs; Schaeffler cuts 3,460 jobs; UK-EU draft food (SPS) deal. Tech (USA): Apple warns of unprecedented memory prices; Google ties Search to AI for schools; CrowdStrike AI kill switch; AI 'slopaganda' political ads. Politics: Americans vote in midterms; US strikes Iran's Qeshm Island; Russia confirms Abu Dhabi talks; Spain's transport minister resigns after crash. Literature (USA): Strand pays $1.5m over PPP loan (not); Chicago's Unabridged changes hands (hot); university presses back Meridian (hot); LitHub 20 new books (hot). Social: New York measles death; Supreme Court on Catholic preschools and LGBTQ parents; US medical debt; UK MPs may face record checks. Sources: The Guardian, CNBC, BBC, NPR, Publishers Weekly, Literary Hub.

stories.headline: US tech stocks bounce back after an AI-spending scare, as Americans vote
stories.dek: The Nasdaq rose 0.83% on Election Day after falling into a 'correction'. Nvidia gained 2.3%, but Apple fell 1.9% because memory chips cost more.
stories.caveman: For about a week, investors had been selling tech and AI stocks. They worried that companies are spending huge sums on AI chips and data centers that may not pay off soon. By Monday, the Nasdaq (a stock index full of tech companies) was in 'correction territory': 10% below its 6 October record. On Tuesday it climbed back 0.83%, and the wider S&P 500 rose 0.37%. Chipmakers led the way: Nvidia gained 2.3% after four down days, and AMD, Broadcom and Micron also jumped. The Dow fell 0.38%, dragged down by Apple, which slipped 1.9% after warning that pricier memory chips will squeeze its profits. Cheaper oil helped the mood: Brent crude fell to $103 a barrel, down from $117 at the end of October, amid talk of new negotiations with Iran and Russia. The midterm elections did not seem to move markets much, though traders expect Democrats to win at least the House, which could mean more AI rules.
stories.why_it_matters: Taiwan's stock market fell sharply the same day on the same AI fears. When US chip stocks swing, Taiwan's market, its currency, and many retirement savings swing with them.
stories.camps: Bulls say AI demand is real and the dip was a normal pause after a big run. Bears say the spending is running ahead of profits and the bounce may not last. Some on the left argue that if Democrats win, stronger AI regulation is overdue; business groups warn too many rules could slow innovation.
stories.image_alt: The Apple flagship store in Hangzhou, China
stories.image_credit: Photo: Long Wei/VCG/Getty Images, via The Guardian

terms.explain: A US stock index packed with tech companies like Apple, Nvidia and Microsoft.
An index of 500 big US companies; a common way to measure 'the market'.
The Dow Jones index of 30 large US companies.
When a stock index falls 10% or more from its recent high.
Chips that store data in phones and computers. AI data centers are buying so many that prices are soaring.
The main international oil price.

stories.headline: Disney plans several thousand layoffs and asks some managers to cut costs by up to 20%
stories.dek: The cuts would come on top of an early-retirement offer from August. Netflix and the newly merged Paramount–Warner Bros. are cutting too.
stories.caveman: Disney, which owns theme parks, Marvel, Pixar, ESPN and the Disney+ streaming service, is preparing to lay off several thousand workers, CNBC reports. Some managers have been told to cut their costs by as much as 20%. It is one of the first big moves by new CEO Josh D'Amaro. In August, Disney offered some staff early retirement and said 'involuntary staff reductions' had already begun and would continue into next year. Disney had about 231,000 employees at the end of its 2025 fiscal year. It is not alone: Netflix said last month it would lay off about 6% of its workforce, and Skydance, the company formed by merging Paramount and Warner Bros. Discovery, is also expected to cut jobs to save $6 billion over three years. Disney reports its next earnings on 17 November.
stories.why_it_matters: Hollywood is shrinking as streaming, merger costs and AI change how films and shows are made. Thousands of creative and office jobs are on the line, not just executives.
stories.camps: Investors often cheer cost cuts because profits can rise. Unions and workers say big media companies keep paying executives well while ordinary staff lose their jobs, and worry AI will be used to replace them. Company leaders argue they must get leaner to compete with tech giants like YouTube and Netflix.
stories.image_alt: A statue of Walt Disney and Mickey Mouse in front of Cinderella Castle at a Disney park

terms.explain: When a company ends people's jobs to save money, not because of their performance.
An offer for older workers to retire sooner, often with extra pay, so the company can shrink.
A company's 12-month accounting year; it doesn't always match the calendar year.
Savings a company expects after a merger, often by cutting overlapping jobs.
A company's quarterly report on how much money it made.

stories.headline: Germany's car industry crisis deepens: parts maker Schaeffler cuts 3,460 jobs and looks to defense
stories.dek: Most of the cuts are in Germany. Europe now sells far fewer new cars than before the pandemic, and Chinese electric cars are pushing in.
stories.caveman: Schaeffler makes parts that go inside cars, like bearings and engine pieces. On Tuesday it said it will cut 3,460 jobs and close or shrink five sites; 2,660 of the jobs are in Germany. By 2028, about 18% of its core German workforce will be gone. Why? Europe is buying far fewer new cars: EU car registrations fell from 15.3 million a year to about 10.8 million. The switch to electric cars also needs fewer parts, and cheaper Chinese EVs are winning customers. Volkswagen, Europe's biggest carmaker, is cutting around 100,000 jobs. Like other German industrial firms, Schaeffler is now looking at the defense industry, where Europe is spending more money, as a new source of business.
stories.why_it_matters: Germany is Europe's biggest economy and its car industry is a key customer for Taiwanese parts and chip makers. When German factories shrink, supply chains far away feel it.
stories.camps: Company leaders say cuts are painful but needed to survive. German unions say workers are paying for bosses' slow move to electric cars and want job guarantees. Some economists argue Europe should protect its car industry from Chinese competition; others say tariffs would make cars more expensive for ordinary buyers.
stories.image_alt: A worker moves an engine at a Volkswagen factory in Zwickau, Germany

terms.explain: A company that makes parts and sells them to carmakers.
The number of new cars officially registered; a way to count car sales.
Electric vehicle: a car that runs on a battery instead of gasoline.
Companies that make weapons and military equipment.
A group of workers who join together to bargain with their employer.

stories.headline: UK and EU agree a draft deal to scrap Brexit red tape on food exports
stories.dek: British sausages, burgers and shellfish could flow to Europe without costly vet checks. In return, Britain would follow EU food rules as they change.
stories.caveman: When Britain left the EU, sending food across the border got hard. Exporters had to pay for vet-signed paperwork, around £200 per health certificate, and their trucks faced checks. Some small firms simply stopped: one yoghurt maker told the BBC it quit exporting because of vets' fees. Now the UK and EU have agreed a draft 'SPS' deal, a 200-page text sent to EU countries this week, ahead of a UK-EU summit later this month. It would remove most of those checks, so fresh sausages, burgers and shellfish could be sold in Europe again. The government says the UK economy could gain £5.1bn a year, and Prime Minister Andy Burnham says up to 0.4% extra on GDP. The catch is 'dynamic alignment': Britain would follow EU food and farming rules, including new ones, without having a vote on them.
stories.why_it_matters: It shows how a country can slowly rebuild trade after a big split. It is also a lesson for any economy, including Taiwan, that trade deals often mean accepting someone else's rules.
stories.camps: Supporters say cheaper, easier trade helps farmers, small businesses and shoppers. Brexit supporters say 'dynamic alignment' means taking orders from Brussels without a say, undoing what voters chose. Others in the middle say the deal is practical, but parliament should be able to review new EU rules.
stories.image_alt: A fisherman sorts his catch on a boat
stories.image_credit: Photo: Chris Ratcliffe/Bloomberg via Getty Images, via BBC

terms.explain: Britain's exit from the European Union, completed in 2020.
Sanitary and phytosanitary rules: food safety and animal and plant health checks.
Annoying paperwork and rules that slow things down.
A document, signed by a vet, proving food is safe to sell abroad.
Agreeing to automatically follow another side's rules, even as they change.
Gross domestic product: the total value of everything an economy produces.

stories.headline: Apple warns of an 'unprecedented' rise in memory chip prices
stories.dek: Revenue beat expectations and Apple raised some prices to cope, but shares still fell. The AI boom is soaking up the world's memory chips.
stories.caveman: Apple reported strong quarterly results: revenue of $114.5bn, up 12% from a year earlier, and earnings of $2.10 per share. But the company, now led by new CEO John Ternus, warned that the price of memory chips is rising at an 'unprecedented' pace. Memory chips store data inside phones and computers. AI data centers are buying enormous amounts of them, so there are fewer left and prices are jumping. That means each iPhone or Mac costs Apple more to make, which squeezes its profit margins. Apple says raising some prices has offset part of the hit. Apple's shares fell 2.75% in after-hours trading, and slid 1.9% the next day.
stories.why_it_matters: If Apple, one of the richest companies on earth, feels the squeeze, everyone does. Phones, laptops and game consoles could get more expensive, and memory makers in Korea and Taiwan are booming.
stories.camps: Investors focused on the margin warning. Fans of Apple note sales are still growing fast. Critics of the AI boom say this is a hidden cost: AI companies' chip buying is pushing up prices for regular consumers.
stories.image_alt: A customer holds the newly launched iPhone Duo at the Apple store on Fifth Avenue in New York
stories.image_credit: Photo: Ryan Murphy/AP, via The Guardian

terms.explain: All the money a company takes in from sales, before costs.
Profit divided by the number of shares; a common way to measure company profit.
How much of each dollar of sales is left as profit.
Buying and selling shares after the main stock market closes.
Never happened before.

stories.headline: Google tells schools: if you switch off our AI, students lose Google Search too
stories.dek: New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani accused Google of using its 'monopoly power to force AI into our public schools'.
stories.caveman: Google announced new AI products for classrooms, plus new controls so schools can limit them. For K-12 student accounts, its Gemini AI tools and Google Search will now be switched off until a school turns them on. But there's a catch: Google says Search and AI are 'deeply integrated', so if a school blocks Google's AI, students also lose Google Search. They will just see a message saying it isn't available. Critics called it a 'hostile ultimatum'. New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani, who recently paused generative AI tools in city schools through eighth grade, said 'no corporation should have the power to dictate how we teach our children.' Former Federal Trade Commission chair Lina Khan said Google was using its search monopoly to 'coerce schools into adopting AI'.
stories.why_it_matters: Students everywhere use Google to do homework. If a single company can say 'take our AI or lose search', schools lose real choice about how kids learn.
stories.camps: Google says it is giving schools more control, not less, and that modern search simply runs on AI. Teachers and parents who worry about AI cheating and learning loss see it as a penalty for saying no. Antitrust critics say this is exactly why big tech monopolies need stronger rules.
stories.image_alt: A Google sign on a building
stories.image_credit: Photo: Gary Hershorn/Getty Images, via The Guardian

terms.explain: US school years from kindergarten to 12th grade, roughly ages 5 to 18.
Google's AI chatbot and family of AI models.
When one company controls almost all of a market, so others can't compete.
A temporary ban or pause.
Federal Trade Commission, the US agency that protects consumers and enforces competition law.
A final demand: do this, or face a bad result.

stories.headline: CrowdStrike launches an 'AI kill switch' to stop company AI agents that go rogue
stories.dek: The tool can cut a misbehaving AI agent off from a company's network, but a human still has to make the call.
stories.caveman: Companies are now using 'AI agents': AI programs that can take actions on their own, like reading files, sending emails or changing systems. What if one goes wrong? Cybersecurity company CrowdStrike launched a 'kill switch' built into its Falcon platform. It can spot what an internal AI agent is doing, stop it, block it from restarting, and cut off its access to the company network. A human must approve the shutdown. CrowdStrike also announced it will work with Anthropic's Claude Cowork tool. Fears are rising after recent incidents, including a July breach at Hugging Face blamed on rogue AI agents and a record crypto hack disclosed by Binance last week. Over the summer, US lawmakers from both parties proposed requiring AI companies to build shutdown abilities into their models. Some critics say one emergency stop button is too simple for huge, connected AI systems.
stories.why_it_matters: As AI starts doing real work, not just chatting, the question 'who can switch it off?' becomes a safety question for banks, hospitals and power grids.
stories.camps: Security companies say kill switches are a basic safety feature, like a circuit breaker. Some engineers doubt one button can control complex systems. Privacy and labor advocates add that the bigger question is how much power companies should give AI agents in the first place.
stories.image_alt: CrowdStrike's CEO speaking at an event

terms.explain: An AI program that can take actions by itself, not just answer questions.
A way to shut something down quickly in an emergency.
Start acting in ways nobody intended or approved.
Protecting computers and networks from hackers and attacks.
A device that cuts off electricity when something goes wrong.
Supported by both major parties, Democrats and Republicans.

stories.headline: AI 'slopaganda' floods US political ads, and there is no federal law to stop it
stories.dek: More than $187m was spent on nearly 300 AI-made election ads. Over 90% of that spending came from the Republican side, a study found.
stories.caveman: 'Slopaganda' mixes 'AI slop' (cheap, fake-looking AI content) and 'propaganda'. Before the midterms, a lot of it showed up in political ads. The Wesleyan Media Project counted more than $187 million spent on nearly 300 ads made or edited with AI, and says that's almost surely too low, because many ads don't say they used AI. Over 90% of the spending came from Republican candidates or groups, and most didn't include a warning label. CNBC found examples like a fake video of New York Democratic Governor Kathy Hochul posted by her Republican opponent. There is no full federal law on AI in political ads; about 30 states have their own rules, but candidates don't always follow them. Platforms like Meta, Google and X are trying to watch for it.
stories.why_it_matters: If voters can't tell a real video from a fake one, elections get harder to trust. The same tools are already used in Taiwan's elections, often by outside actors.
stories.camps: Supporters of regulation want clear labels and a federal law. Free-speech advocates warn that banning political ads, even fake ones, could be abused to silence criticism and satire. Republicans who use AI ads say they are just a cheaper way to make campaign content; critics say spreading fakes about opponents crosses a line no matter who does it.
stories.image_alt: Political candidates speaking at campaign events

terms.explain: AI 'slop' plus propaganda: cheap, fake AI content used to push a political message.
Low-quality content mass-produced with AI.
Information, often misleading, spread to push people toward a political view.
A label telling viewers that AI was used.
A fake video or audio made with AI that looks real.
A national law in the US, passed by Congress, rather than a state law.

stories.headline: Americans vote in midterm elections seen as a referendum on Trump
stories.dek: Control of the House and Senate, both held by Republicans, is at stake. Results were not yet known when this issue was made.
stories.caveman: On Tuesday 3 November, Americans voted in the 'midterms', elections held halfway through a president's four-year term. All of the House of Representatives and about a third of the Senate are on the ballot, plus 36 governors and many local offices and ballot questions. Republicans control both houses of Congress now. Trump made himself the center of the race, holding dozens of rallies and telling supporters to vote as if his name were on the ballot. The party in the White House usually loses seats in midterms. Polls suggested Democrats were well placed to win the House; the Senate was harder, because many seats up for grabs are in states Trump won. Democrats focused on the cost of living; Republicans on Trump's agenda. Note: results were still coming in when this issue was put together, so check live results for who won.
stories.why_it_matters: Congress decides budgets, laws and investigations. Who controls it decides how much of Trump's agenda, on immigration, the Iran war, tariffs, can move forward in his last two years.
stories.camps: Democrats framed the vote as a check on a president whose power has gone largely unchecked. Republicans said voters should reward Trump's agenda and that Democrats offer no clear plan. Independents in polls mostly said prices and jobs mattered most.
stories.image_alt: Voters fill out ballots on the last day of early voting in Detroit, Michigan
stories.image_credit: Photo: Sarah Yenesel/EPA, via The Guardian

terms.explain: US elections held two years into a president's term.
Here: a vote treated as a thumbs up or down on one person or idea.
The bigger chamber of Congress; all 435 seats are elected every two years.
The smaller chamber of Congress, with 100 senators; about a third are elected every two years.
A big win for Democrats (whose color is blue).
A question voters decide directly, like a new law.

stories.headline: US strikes Iran's Qeshm Island in what officials call a limited, defensive attack
stories.dek: The strikes came after Iran's Revolutionary Guards fired on a US aircraft. Mediators from Qatar and Pakistan are trying to prevent a return to all-out war.
stories.caveman: The US and Israel went to war with Iran in February. Now there is an uneasy pause, with talks on and off. On Monday, the US hit Qeshm Island, in the narrow Strait of Hormuz where much of the world's oil passes, US officials told CBS. They called the strikes 'limited and defensive', a response to Iran's Revolutionary Guards firing on a US aircraft. Iran's state media reported explosions; the Guards said they shot down three US drones. Trump, facing falling polls and pressure from his own party to end the war, said he was in 'no rush' to escalate and that Iran is crippled financially, but also floated hitting an underground nuclear-linked site. Iran's parliament speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf said the 'ball is in America's court'. Qatar and Pakistan are mediating.
stories.why_it_matters: Any fighting near the Strait of Hormuz pushes up oil prices worldwide, including what Taiwan pays for fuel and electricity.
stories.camps: The US government calls the strikes self-defense. Iran calls them aggression. Many Democrats and some Republicans want Congress to have a say and want the war ended; hawks argue pressure is what brings Iran to the table.
stories.image_alt: Ships at sea seen from a beach in the Gulf region

terms.explain: A narrow sea passage next to Iran; about a fifth of the world's oil passes through it.
Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, a powerful military force loyal to Iran's supreme leader.
An aircraft with no pilot on board, flown remotely.
Make a conflict bigger or more intense.
A neutral party that helps two sides talk and reach a deal.

stories.headline: Russia confirms new Ukraine peace talks in Abu Dhabi as Melania Trump prepares to host a ceasefire meeting
stories.dek: Talks are set for 10–11 November. Zelenskyy insists nothing about Ukraine can be decided without Ukraine at the table.
stories.caveman: Russia says it will send negotiators to Abu Dhabi, in the United Arab Emirates, on 10 and 11 November for new talks about ending the war in Ukraine. Vladimir Medinsky, a Kremlin adviser who led Russia's team in earlier talks, will lead again. Separately, First Lady Melania Trump is set to host a meeting on Thursday about a ceasefire around Kherson, a front-line region in southern Ukraine. There is also talk of a possible meeting between Putin, Trump and China's Xi Jinping. Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskyy welcomed efforts for peace but said Kyiv must be at the table for any deal about its future.
stories.why_it_matters: Russia's war is the biggest in Europe since World War II. How it ends, and whether big powers decide for smaller countries, matters a lot for Taiwan too.
stories.camps: Supporters of quick talks say every month of war costs thousands of lives. Ukraine and many European allies fear a deal made over Ukraine's head would reward invasion. Skeptics note Russia has joined talks before while continuing heavy attacks.
stories.image_alt: First Lady Melania Trump at a White House event

terms.explain: An agreement to stop fighting, at least for a while.
Russia's government, named after its headquarters in Moscow.
The capital of the United Arab Emirates, often used for neutral talks.
A region in southern Ukraine, partly occupied by Russia.
The capital of Ukraine; also used to mean Ukraine's government.

stories.headline: Spain's transport minister resigns after a train crash that killed at least 69 people
stories.dek: Óscar Puente said no minister could stay after two disasters on the same line in under a year. Spain votes on 29 November.
stories.caveman: Last Wednesday, near the town of Urda south of Madrid, a high-speed train smashed into the back of a train that was standing still. At least 69 people died and dozens were hurt. It was Spain's worst rail crash since 2013 and one of Europe's worst in modern times. In January, another crash on the same line killed 46 people. On Tuesday, after hours of questions in parliament, Transport Minister Óscar Puente resigned. 'A transport minister in a country like Spain cannot remain in office after two accidents of this seriousness in less than a year,' he said. Opposition parties and even some government allies had demanded he go. Investigators are still working out exactly why the trains collided. Spain holds a general election on 29 November.
stories.why_it_matters: When public services fail, people want someone to take responsibility. Rail safety is also a real issue for Taiwan, where trains carry millions every day.
stories.camps: Opposition parties say the resignation came too late and the government ignored warnings after January. The governing Socialists say Puente did the honorable thing and the focus should now be on finding the cause. Rail unions point to years of underinvestment in maintenance under several governments.
stories.image_alt: Óscar Puente speaking in Spain's Congress

terms.explain: Quit a job, usually after pressure or a scandal.
A train that runs at 250 km/h or faster, like Taiwan's HSR.
A senior government official in charge of one area, like transport.
A national election that chooses a new parliament and government.
Not spending enough money to keep something safe and working.

stories.headline: NOT: New York's Strand bookstore pays nearly $1.5m to settle a case over its Covid loan
stories.dek: Prosecutors said owner Nancy Bass Wyden, wife of Senator Ron Wyden, wrongly certified the store was eligible. The Strand calls it an honest mistake.
stories.caveman: The Strand, the famous New York bookstore known for its '18 miles of books', will pay $1,482,560 to settle a case about a $932,350 Covid relief loan it got in 2021. The loans came from the Paycheck Protection Program (PPP), meant to help small businesses keep paying workers during the pandemic. But Congress had banned businesses controlled by a spouse of a member of Congress from the second round of loans. Owner Nancy Bass Wyden is married to Ron Wyden, a Democratic senator from Oregon. The office of US Attorney Jeanine Pirro said her signed statement on the application was 'knowingly and materially false'. The Strand said it was an 'unintentional' mistake and it didn't know about the rule. The settlement makes no finding that the store is liable.
stories.why_it_matters: The Strand is one of America's best-known independent bookstores. It is also a political story: Wyden is a fierce Trump critic, and Pirro was appointed by Trump.
stories.camps: Prosecutors say rules apply to everyone, including families of powerful lawmakers. The Strand's defenders say it was a paperwork error during a crisis, and some see politics in a Trump appointee targeting a critic's family. Both can be true: the rule existed, and the case is also political.
stories.image_alt: Strand owner Nancy Bass Wyden with Strand books and merchandise on a TV set

terms.explain: Paycheck Protection Program: US government loans during Covid that could be forgiven if businesses kept paying workers.
End a legal case by agreeing to pay or do something, without a trial.
Legal responsibility for doing something wrong.
A federal prosecutor in charge of one region.
Officially state that something is true.

stories.headline: HOT: Chicago's gay-owned Unabridged Bookstore changes hands after 46 years, and sales are up 40%
stories.dek: Founder Ed Devereux sold the Boystown shop to Shane Khosropour, its chief book buyer for more than 20 years,, who promises to keep its famous LGBTQ section.
stories.caveman: Unabridged Bookstore opened in 1980 in Chicago's Lakeview neighborhood, in the area known as Boystown, the heart of the city's gay community. Founder Ed Devereux built it as a general bookstore with a big selection of gay and lesbian books. On 1 October, after 46 years, he sold it to Shane Khosropour, the store's chief book buyer, who has worked there for more than 20 years. Devereux will stay involved informally, reading and recommending books. Khosropour says the LGBTQ section is 'the best in the country, sort of a store-within-a-store', and he doesn't plan big changes: 'I'm just planning on keeping it open and relevant, and a welcoming place.' Good news for indie bookshops: Devereux told PW this spring that sales were up 40% over 2025, and the store was a finalist for PW's 2026 Bookstore of the Year.
stories.why_it_matters: Independent bookstores, especially LGBTQ ones, are community spaces as much as shops. A smooth handover to someone who already loves the store is the best way to keep one alive.
stories.camps: Supporters say queer bookstores matter more now, as some US states ban LGBTQ books from schools and libraries. Others note indie shops still face tough competition from Amazon and rising rents, so one success story doesn't fix the business.
stories.image_alt: Storefront buildings on a Chicago street

terms.explain: An independently owned bookstore, not part of a big chain.
A neighborhood in Chicago known as the center of its LGBTQ community.
Lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender and queer people.
Gets a new owner.
Removing books from schools or libraries, often LGBTQ or race-related titles.

stories.headline: HOT: Three top university presses back Meridian, a service that lets AI tools cite real scholarly books
stories.dek: Cambridge, Johns Hopkins and Princeton are founding publishers. The content can't be used to train AI models.
stories.caveman: When students ask AI chatbots questions, the answers often come from random websites, or are made up. Meridian, a new service from Salt Lake City start-up Cashmere, wants to fix that. Cambridge University Press, Johns Hopkins University Press and Princeton University Press are its first partners. When a researcher asks an AI tool a question, Meridian lets the tool pull its answer from peer-reviewed books and journals the person's library already pays for, cite the source, and send them to the published version. The content cannot be used to train AI models or be resold. It uses MCP, an open standard created by Anthropic that lets AI assistants connect to outside databases. Cashmere raised $5 million earlier this year.
stories.why_it_matters: It's a test of whether publishers and authors can get paid, and get credit, in the AI age, instead of having their work scraped for free.
stories.camps: Publishers say this protects authors' work while helping students find reliable sources. Some authors' groups remain wary of any AI deals and want stronger consent and payment. AI optimists say better sources make AI answers more accurate for everyone.
stories.image_alt: Portrait photo accompanying PW's report on Meridian

terms.explain: A publisher run by a university, mostly for academic books.
Checked by other experts before being published.
Feed huge amounts of text into an AI model so it learns patterns.
Model Context Protocol: an open standard that lets AI assistants connect to other tools and databases.
Name where information came from.

stories.headline: HOT: 20 new books out today, from Tom Drury, Elizabeth McCracken, Louise Kennedy and more
stories.dek: Literary Hub's weekly list for 3 November includes Drury's 'West of Loveland' and McCracken's 'Seven Stories About Tammy'.
stories.caveman: Every Tuesday is release day for new books in the US, and Literary Hub rounds up the ones worth noticing. This week's list of 20 includes new fiction from Tom Drury, a cult favorite known for quiet, funny novels set in small-town Midwest America ('West of Loveland'); Elizabeth McCracken, a prize-winning writer of sharp, tender short fiction ('Seven Stories About Tammy'); and Louise Kennedy, the Irish writer whose earlier novel 'Trespasses' was a big hit, with 'Stations'. The list mixes novels, story collections and nonfiction. Good starting points if you want something new to read this month.
stories.why_it_matters: Release-day lists help readers spot new books before they become famous, and show which writers critics are excited about right now.
stories.camps: Lists like this lean toward literary fiction from established writers. Some readers and critics want more space for debut authors, translated books and writers of color; LitHub's lists usually include some, but big names get the headline.
stories.image_alt: Illustrated cover art from one of this week's new books

terms.explain: The day a new book officially goes on sale; in the US it's usually Tuesday.
A writer or work with a small but very devoted fan base.
A book made up of several short stories.
Fiction focused on style and character more than plot formulas.
A writer's first book.

stories.headline: A New York child dies of measles, the state's first measles death in 30 years
stories.dek: Governor Kathy Hochul blamed Washington for 'deliberately' eroding vaccine protections. US cases this year are more than double last year's.
stories.caveman: Measles is a very contagious virus. It can cause fever, rash, pneumonia and brain swelling, and kills about one to three of every 1,000 people who catch it. A vaccine prevents it, and the US had stopped local spread back in 2000. But vaccination rates have dropped below the 95% needed to stop outbreaks. Now a child in Lewis County, in rural northern New York, has died after catching measles, the state's first measles death in 30 years. Governor Kathy Hochul said she was heartbroken and blamed the federal government for 'deliberately' eroding progress on vaccines. The CDC counted 4,588 US measles cases in 2026 by late October, more than double 2025; Pennsylvania alone reported 1,338. In October Hochul declared a disaster emergency so more health workers could give measles shots.
stories.why_it_matters: Diseases that were nearly gone can come back fast when fewer people vaccinate. Children too young for shots, or with weak immune systems, are the most at risk.
stories.camps: Public health experts and Democrats blame the federal health department under Robert F Kennedy Jr for spreading doubt about vaccines. RFK Jr and his supporters say they are giving parents more choice and information. Doctors in both parties stress the measles vaccine is safe and highly effective.
stories.image_alt: A vial of measles, mumps and rubella vaccine

stories.headline: Supreme Court leans toward letting taxpayer-funded Catholic preschools turn away children of LGBTQ parents
stories.dek: Colorado's free pre-K program bans discrimination. The Denver archdiocese says that violates its religious freedom.
stories.caveman: In 2022, Colorado started paying for preschool for every four-year-old, about $6,300 per child per year. Religious schools can join, but they must follow the state's anti-discrimination law. The Catholic Archdiocese of Denver wants the money but also wants to refuse children whose parents are gay or transgender. It says the rule violates its constitutional right to practice religion freely. (Catholic Charities and some other Catholic groups in the state do follow the rules.) At the Supreme Court on Tuesday, the conservative majority seemed ready to side with the archdiocese; Justice Neil Gorsuch suggested Colorado was ignoring earlier rulings on religious freedom. The three liberal justices strongly disagreed: Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson compared it to a school refusing the children of Black people on religious grounds, and Justice Sonia Sotomayor pressed the archdiocese's lawyer on the fact that its school could reject a child because of the parents. Colorado argued that public money should serve all families equally. A decision is expected by summer 2027.
stories.why_it_matters: This decides how far religious freedom goes when public money is involved, and whether children of LGBTQ families can be shut out of programs every taxpayer funds.
stories.camps: Religious-liberty supporters say the state can't force faith schools to act against their beliefs to get the same funding as others. LGBTQ advocates and Colorado say taxpayer money must not be used to discriminate against small children. Legal experts note the court has steadily expanded religious rights in recent years.
stories.image_alt: The US Supreme Court in Washington, D.C.
stories.image_credit: Photo: Saul Loeb/AFP via Getty Images, via NPR

stories.headline: Millions of Americans are still crushed by medical debt, even as charities wipe some away
stories.dek: Americans owed at least $220bn in medical debt in 2024. Experts say forgiveness helps, but the real problem is healthcare people can't afford.
stories.caveman: In the US, getting sick can mean getting a huge bill. Even people with insurance often have to pay a lot before coverage kicks in. In 2024, Americans owed at least $220bn in medical debt, according to the research group KFF; about 14 million people owed more than $1,000 and 3 million owed more than $10,000. One in five households had an overdue medical bill. Charities like Undue Medical Debt buy old debt from hospitals and collectors very cheaply (a $1 donation wipes out about $100 of debt) and then cancel it. Relief has grown a lot this year. But experts say it's a bandage: people keep falling into debt because care costs too much.
stories.why_it_matters: Taiwan's national health insurance means most people never see bills like this. Comparing the two shows why health systems are a big political fight in the US.
stories.camps: Progressives say the fix is universal coverage, like 'Medicare for All', and strict limits on prices. Conservatives prefer more competition and price transparency, and warn government-run care would raise taxes. Most people across parties agree that surprise bills and aggressive debt collection are unfair.

stories.headline: UK MPs could face criminal record checks under a plan to stop violence against women in Parliament
stories.dek: Parliament becomes the first legislature in the world with 'White Ribbon' accreditation, promising a three-year plan to change its culture.
stories.caveman: Britain's Parliament has a long reputation for sexism and harassment: long late-night hours, lots of bars on site, and staff who work directly for powerful MPs with little HR help. A 2018 survey found nearly 20% of people there had experienced or seen sexual harassment. Now, after a cross-party campaign led by Labour MP Emily Darlington and backed by the Speaker, Lindsay Hoyle, Parliament is getting 'White Ribbon' accreditation, a culture-change program that started in Canada. The three-year plan is expected to include 'bystander training' (how to spot and step in when you see harassment), higher behavior standards for MPs and peers, and possibly criminal record checks for new MPs before they get a security pass.
stories.why_it_matters: When lawmakers make rules for everyone else, their own workplace should be safe too. It's a model other parliaments, including Taiwan's Legislative Yuan, could look at.
stories.camps: Campaigners say checks and training are overdue. Some MPs worry about fairness and privacy, and argue voters, not background checks, should decide who serves. Others say the details matter: training only works if complaints are taken seriously and abusers face real consequences.
